title: Reclaiming languages and cultures

draft.title: Reclaiming languages and cultures
card: Before colonisation, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples spoke hundreds of languages. Colonisation suppressed many of them, and cultural practices such as ceremony were also restricted.
Policies that removed children from their families, and that stopped children speaking language at missions and schools, broke the passing on of language and culture between generations.
Today Aboriginal communities are reviving languages and cultural practices. They record words from elders and old sources, run language classes and teach culture to young people.
Language and culture carry knowledge, stories and law, and link people to Country. Reviving them can strengthen identity and a sense of belonging.
draft.remember: Colonisation suppressed languages and cultures. Communities are now reviving them, which strengthens identity and connection to Country.

a.q: Why did many Aboriginal languages stop being passed on to children?
opts: Colonial policies broke links between generations
Communities chose to adopt English for every purpose
Languages had no stories or knowledge to pass on
Elders stopped wanting to teach young people
a.why: Removing children from families and stopping them speaking language at missions and schools broke the passing on of language. It was not a free choice by communities, and languages carry knowledge and stories.
a.clue: Think about what happened to children under past policies.

b.q: A community in NSW runs weekly classes where elders teach young people words in their local language. What is the main effect this can have?
opts: It can strengthen identity and connection to Country
It ends the need to record language from elders
It brings back the policies that once suppressed language
It makes every community speak one shared language
b.why: Learning language from elders passes on knowledge and links young people to Country, which can strengthen identity. The classes do not replace elders, and they do not create one shared language, since each community has its own.
b.clue: Language carries stories and ties people to Country.

a.best: Colonial policies broke links between generations

b.best: It can strengthen identity and connection to Country

a.q: Why did many Aboriginal languages stop being passed on to children?
opts: Colonial policies broke links between generations
Communities chose to adopt English for every purpose
Elders stopped wanting to teach young people
Languages were never used outside of ceremony
a.why: Removing children from families and stopping them speaking language at missions and schools broke the passing on of language. It was not a free choice by communities or elders, and languages were used in daily life, carrying knowledge, stories and law.
a.clue: Think about what happened to children under past policies.

b.q: A community in NSW runs weekly classes where elders teach young people words in their local language. What can these classes do?
opts: It can strengthen identity and connection to Country
It can give the community legal ownership of its land
It can stop young people from needing to speak English
It can reverse the past removal of children from families
b.why: Language carries knowledge, stories and law and links people to Country, so learning it from elders can strengthen identity and belonging. Language classes do not change who legally owns land, which is a separate matter of law. They also cannot undo past policies or replace English in daily life.
b.clue: Think about what language carries and what it links people to.
